summary: Cardona Island Light guards the western side of Ponce Harbor from a six-acre key: built by the Spanish, finished in 1889, automated in 1962, condemned after 2020 earthquake damage.

lens.where: The sources disagree on whether the original sixth-order lens is still in place; see notes_for_editor.

structures.note: 31 ft high from its base in the 1901 Lighthouse Board report; the 1981 nomination gives 10 m.
Designed for one second-class keeper; blue with white trimmings in 1901, white by 1925.
Finished early in 1914 at a cost of $370.72 (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Coast Guard property on a six-acre key, reached only by private boat. The US Lighthouse Society archive lists it as not open to the public. The Coast Guard revoked the certificate of occupancy and condemned the facility in March 2021; entry is prohibited.

events.note: Tower begun in 1887 and finished in 1889 by the Spanish, at a cost of 11,760 pesos
Original sixth-order lens. The Coast Guard list gives 1889; the 1981 nomination gives 1888.
Relighted on the evening of 29 July 1898, per the Army report on its Puerto Rico operations as quoted by LighthouseFriends
Reinforced-concrete oil house finished at a cost of $370.72

A hurricane passed over Puerto Rico in September 1921; the Bulletin lists Cardona Island among the ninth-district stations damaged. Its figures (four boats lost, many station buildings damaged) are for the group.
Changed from fixed red to flashing white; oil to acetylene at a cost of $1,025
Tower and dwelling painted white by 16 February 1925
White flash every 4 seconds from 14 July 1937
Electric powered illumination from 11 April 1962; the nomination says electrified and apparently unmanned in 1962
Disputed: the Puerto Rico record says a sixth-order lens was in use until 1978 when it was substituted; LighthouseFriends says the original was still in use in the late 1970s
Included in the National Register in 1981 (PRAHA record). NPGallery gives the nomination's 'Date Published' as 22 October 1981, an asset date that may differ from the listing date.
Significant damage from the 2020 earthquake and seismic activity
Certificate of occupancy revoked and facility condemned, 22 March 2021; entry prohibited

corrections.why: The 1901 Lighthouse Board report gives the tower as 31 feet high from its base, and the USLHS place record gives 31 ft (tower_height_ft). 11 m (36 ft) is in neither; the 1981 nomination gives 10 m.
USLHS lists it as not open to the public; the Coast Guard revoked the certificate of occupancy and condemned the tower in March 2021 and says entry is prohibited.

The sources disagree: the Puerto Rico record says the lens was substituted in 1978; LighthouseFriends says it is now in a Coast Guard museum in San Juan; the 1981 nomination says it was still in use. Needs a site check or a Coast Guard answer.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1901 Lighthouse Board report says the tower was begun in 1887 and finished in 1889 by the Spanish. 1889 is the completion year used by the Coast Guard list and the record.

The 1901 report and the 1981 nomination describe a fixed red light. The Coast Guard list records flashing white from 25 May 1922 and a 4-second flash from 14 July 1937. The record's Fl W 4s is the 1937 characteristic.

notes_for_editor: (1) The keeper names and dates come from the USLHS place record, which prints the NARA register roster (via Kraig Anderson's inventory). roster.py 2026-10-27 prints the same seven lines; the role 'keeper' (not 'head keeper') is roster.py's rule for a station with no assistants, and the dwelling was built for one keeper. No keeper was checked against a primary register; 'at least' marks a documented span. Names matched by the archive, not by position. Simeon Martin's archive person slug also covers the Cabo Rojo stint (1901-1902); not verified as one man in a primary record. (2) Lens: three sources disagree. The nomination (published 1981 per NPGallery) says the 1888 lens was still in use; the PRAHA record says a sixth-order lens was substituted in 1978 and calls the lens 'works with solar panels' (unclear, not used); LighthouseFriends says the lens is in the Coast Guard museum in San Juan. Not verified on site. (3) Dates: the PRAHA record says the station was closed in 1950; the Coast Guard list shows only the 1942-43 wartime darkness and no 1950 closure. Left out of the story as a disputed date, but stated as the record's claim. Wikipedia gives 1942/1943 with a citation to the nomination; the cached nomination has only pp. 29-30 of 47, so the Wikipedia claim was not used. (4) The 1921 hurricane: the OCR of the Bulletin reads 'On September () and LO , 1921'. The PDF page image (PDF page 37, printed page 197) reads 'On September 9 and 10, 1921' and 'Four boats were lost'; the story uses the month only, which the OCR text supports. The damage figures are for the group of stations, not Cardona alone. (5) Tower height: 31 ft (1901 report, USLHS tower height) against 10 m (nomination) and 11 m (record); the story states the disagreement and gives 33 ft (10 m) from the nomination. (6) The 1898 relighting is second-hand: the Army report is quoted by LighthouseFriends; the primary report was not located. (7) LighthouseFriends says 'Grounds open, tower closed'; the Coast Guard's 2021 release describes fencing and signs about 50 feet from the tower, so the story does not say grounds are open. (8) Printed page numbers for the 1901 Lighthouse Board report (scan pp. 106, 108) were not read; cited by scan page. (9) 'Last century' in the nomination (1981) is read as the 19th century, as the nomination's own periods of significance (1875-1899) suggest; the story says 'the nineteenth century, the nomination says'. (10) The PRAHA record's description is compiled from a Facebook page, and its editor is Fundación Luis Muñoz Marín; it is cited as a drawings-archive record, not as an official record. (11) Fact-check 2026-10-22: quotes re-checked (56 found on the first run); story sentences checked against the NRHP pages, USLHS place record, LighthouseFriends, the USCG light list, the 1901 Lighthouse Board report scan pages 106 and 108, the 1921 and 1922 Bulletins, the FY1922 Commissioner report (scan p. 748, printed p. 48), the 2021 Coast Guard release, the PRAHA record and the NPGallery asset record.
